title: The New Turing Omnibus
body:
A. K. Dewdney's *The New Turing Omnibus* holds 66 short chapters, each a self-contained tour
of one idea in computing, assuming nothing from the chapters around it. Theory, hardware and
graphics are interleaved deliberately, so the book can be opened anywhere.

Nobody reads it in order, so this note is organised by which course each chapter feeds. The
Omnibus gives a topic its short motivated version and the course gives it the long one, and
several chapters cover ground no course in the degree reaches at all. This is the only folder
in the vault holding no course, and it is the one that ties the others together, because
almost every note here links into several course folders at once.

## Topics

### Computability and formal languages

The largest block, and a compressed version of [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].
The machines themselves live in that folder and these notes own the classification and the
limits.

[[Chomsky Hierarchy]] is the organising table for the subject. Four classes of [[Languages]]
nest strictly inside one another, and each class is defined three ways at once, by a grammar
shape, by a machine, and by how much memory that machine has:

```
regular             finite automaton            states only
context-free        pushdown automaton          one stack
context-sensitive   linear bounded automaton    tape bounded by the input
recursively enum.   Turing machine              unbounded tape
```

Each level is strictly larger than the one below, proved by exhibiting a language in the
higher class and absent from the lower one. [[Regular Languages]] is the bottom rung, the class
a fixed amount of memory can decide, and the [[DFA]], [[NFA]], [[Regular Expressions]] and
[[Pumping Lemma]] notes cover the machinery. [[Automata]] indexes the machine ladder.

[[Nondeterminism]] asks the question the ladder keeps returning to: whether letting a machine
guess adds power. For finite automata the answer is no, since the subset construction
converts any NFA to a DFA. For the [[Turing Machine]] the answer is no. For [[NP-Complete]]
problems the answer is unknown, and that open question is P against NP.

[[Godel's Theorem]] is the logic half of [[Undecidability]], produced by the same
self-reference argument five years earlier. [[Systems of Logic]] sets it up, defining a formal
system as symbols with axioms and inference rules, and separating soundness, meaning everything
provable is true, from completeness, meaning everything true is provable. First-order logic is
complete and arithmetic is incomplete, and both results are Gödel's, about different systems,
which is the confusion the note exists to prevent.

[[Simulation]] carries both senses of its word, one machine imitating another as a proof
technique, and modelling a physical system numerically. The note keeps them apart.

### Data structures and algorithms

Feeds [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]. Each note maps
over notes living in those folders and adds one argument the individual notes leave out.

[[Search Trees]] covers every [[Tree]] whose shape encodes an ordering, where
[[Binary Search Tree]] owns the invariant, [[Balanced Tree]] owns the rotations, [[Heap]] owns
the member that orders only the root, and [[Hashing]] is the alternative that abandons order
entirely to buy constant-time lookup.

[[Sequential Sorting]] maps [[Bubble Sort]], [[Insertion Sort]], [[Merge Sort]] and
[[Quick Sort]], and carries the lower bound none of them states. A comparison sort is a
decision tree with two outcomes per comparison, so a tree of height $h$ distinguishes at most
$2^h$ orderings, and reaching all $n!$ of them forces $h \geq \log_2(n!) = \Theta(n \log n)$.
The wall is a fact about information and no implementation crosses it.

[[Minimum Spanning Tree]] is the classic greedy result on a [[Weighted Graph]]: connect every
vertex, use no cycles, minimise the total weight. A spanning tree of $V$ vertices always has
exactly $V - 1$ edges, since the first edge connects two vertices and each additional edge
adds one more without closing a loop. Greedy fails on most problems and succeeds here, and
both Kruskal and Prim carry proofs.

[[Game Trees]] covers search where an opponent chooses half the moves. Minimax evaluates a
tree of $O(b^d)$ nodes for branching factor $b$ and depth $d$, which is hopeless past a few
plies, and alpha-beta pruning cuts that to $O(b^{d/2})$ with good move ordering by abandoning
any branch already proved worse than one examined. That square root is the difference between
searching 8 plies and 16. The static evaluation function scores a position the search never
reaches the end of, and the horizon effect is what happens when a disaster sits one ply past
the depth limit. [[Algorithm]], [[Asymptotic Analysis]] and [[Recursion]] are the earlier notes
this block assumes.

### Hardware and digital logic

Feeds [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] and [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]].

[[Karnaugh Maps]] is graphical minimisation of a Boolean expression. The axes are Gray-coded,
so adjacent cells differ in exactly one variable, which turns algebraic cancellation into
visible adjacency:

```
        B=0  B=1
 A=0     0    1
 A=1     0    1        the two 1s are adjacent, and they differ only in A

 F = A'B + AB = B(A' + A) = B        one gate, down from three
```

Grouping the ones in blocks of a power of two and reading off the terms produces a minimal
expression, and fewer terms means fewer gates on the board. [[Boolean Algebra]] holds the
identities behind it, and [[Digital circuit]], [[Combinational Logic]], [[Encoder]],
[[Multiplexer]] and [[Decoder]] are what gets minimised.

[[Error Correcting Code]] is the middle rung of the vault's three-part error story, where
[[Error Detection]] notices a fault, this repairs it, and [[Finite Field]] explains why the
algebra works. The governing quantity is Hamming distance, the number of positions in which
two codewords differ. Detecting a single error needs a minimum distance of 2, and correcting
$t$ errors needs $2t + 1$, so that any word within $t$ flips of a codeword is closer to that
codeword than to any other.

```
Hamming(7,4): four data bits, three parity bits, each covering a different subset

data 1011  ->  codeword 0 1 1 0 0 1 1
                        p p d p d d d      positions 1..7

flip position 5:        0 1 1 0 1 1 1
recompute the three parity checks:  they fail on 1, 4 and 5
                                    1 + 4 = 5, which names the broken bit
```

The parity bits are placed at powers of two precisely so the failing checks add up to the
position of the error, which is why the code locates the error and can therefore repair it. Hamming
codes repair single bits, and Reed-Solomon over $GF(2^8)$ repairs whole [[Byte|bytes]], which
is what lets it survive a scratch that destroys a run of adjacent bits. A CD, a QR code and a
RAID array all run this quietly.

### Numerical and graphical methods

Feeds the math block, mostly [[CALCULUS 1]] and [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]].

[[Spline Curves]] fits a smooth curve through a set of points by chaining low-degree
polynomials, because a single polynomial through $n$ points has degree $n-1$ and oscillates
wildly between them. Cubic is the lowest degree reaching $C^2$ continuity at the joins,
meaning the position, the slope and the curvature all match, which is what makes the joint
invisible. The coefficients come from a tridiagonal system, and Bezier curves are the
graphics-facing version behind every font outline and easing function.

[[Random Numbers]] covers what a deterministic machine can produce, which is a fully determined
sequence that passes statistical tests for randomness. The same seed gives the same sequence,
and that reproducibility is what makes [[Simulation]] debuggable and a game replayable.
Cryptography sets a higher bar, requiring that the next value stay unpredictable to somebody
who has seen every previous one, which [[Stream Cipher]] in [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] covers.
[[Cryptography]] here is a pointer note, since the book gives the subject one chapter and Cryptography gives it a term.

### Neural networks and vision

The largest block by note count, written jointly with [[MACHINE LEARNING]] because the material
is one topic split across two folders. The Omnibus chapter is a 1989 introduction to the
[[Perceptron]], and everything following from it is modern.

[[Perceptron]] is a single unit computing a weighted sum and thresholding it, and the note
carries what one unit cannot do. A single perceptron draws one straight line through the input
space and labels the two sides, so it can compute AND and OR and it cannot compute XOR:

```
XOR:   (0,0) -> 0     (1,1) -> 0        the two 0s are diagonally opposite
       (0,1) -> 1     (1,0) -> 1        so is the pair of 1s

no straight line separates one diagonal pair from the other
```

That observation stalled the field for a decade, and the [[Multilayer Perceptron]] resolves it,
since a hidden layer bends the boundary. [[Neural Network]] is the hub, linking [[Neuron]],
[[Input Layer]], [[Hidden Layer]], [[Output Layer]], [[Weights]] and [[Bias Term]].

[[Forward Pass]] is matrix multiplication, which is [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] doing the work.
[[Back Propagation]] is the [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] evaluated backwards, and
[[Gradient Descent]] is [[Optimization]] with too many variables for a closed form. None of
that is new mathematics, which is the useful thing to know before reading a paper about it.

[[Activation Function]] supplies the [[Non-Linear|non-linearity]] without which stacked layers
collapse into one, through [[Sigmoid]], [[ReLU]] and [[Leaky ReLU]]. [[Loss Function]] and
[[Log Loss]] are what gets minimised, with [[Logistic Regression]] as the smallest model
requiring gradient descent. [[CNN]] and [[Convolutional Neural Network]] handle images by
sharing weights across positions, and [[Computer Vision]] states the problem: an image is a
[[Matrix]] of intensities and no formula takes pixels to meaning.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] covers the theory block above from the course
  side.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] and [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] cover the trees,
  sorting, graphs and the complexity arguments over them.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] and [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] cover logic
  minimisation and the detection end of the error story.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] and [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] supply the
  [[Finite Field]] algebra under [[Error Correcting Code]], and
  [[Post-Quantum Cryptography]] turns decoding back into a hardness assumption.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE]] continue the neural network block, and
  [[Game Trees]] is the classical AI chapter that predates it.
- [[CALCULUS 1]], [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]], [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] and
  [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] supply the splines, the gradients and the matrix view of
  a network.
- [[STATISTICS]] and [[DISCRETE MATH]] supply the [[Probability]]
  under random number generation and the [[Proof]] under the logic block.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] supplies [[Recursion]] and [[Algorithm]],
  which nearly everything here assumes.
